## S1 Derivation of the mesoscopic model

### S1.1 Mori–Zwanzig formalism

We consider a general state space and the autonomous deterministic dynamics on it,

$$ \dot{\mathbf{Z}}(t)=\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{Z}(t)),\qquad\mathbf{Z}(0)=\mathbf{z}, $$

where $\mathbf{z}$ is a microstate of the state space. We are interested in the dynamics of the observable $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})=(A_{1}(\mathbf{z}),\ldots,A_{m}(\mathbf{z}))$ , and write $\mathbf{A}(t)=\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{Z}(t))$ . The components $A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}$ are assumed functionally independent, with no identity relating them as functions of $\mathbf{z}$ [1]. By the chain rule,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbf{A}(t)=\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{Z}(t))\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{Z}(t))=(\mathcal{L}\mathbf{A})(\mathbf{Z}(t)),\qquad\mathcal{L}f(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{z})\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}f(\mathbf{z}), $$

where $\mathcal{L}$ is the Liouville operator, the generator of the flow on observables, so that $\mathbf{A}(t)=(e^{t\mathcal{L}}\mathbf{A})(\mathbf{z})$ . Let $\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}(\mathbf{z})$ be an invariant probability distribution, so that $\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}\cdot(\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}\mathbf{G})=0$ and, for every admissible observable $f$ ,

$$ \int\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}(\mathbf{z})\,\mathcal{L}f(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}=0. $$

Equation 1 follows from the stationarity of $\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}$ by the divergence theorem provided the flux $\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}f\mathbf{G}$ vanishes on the boundary of the state space and at infinity. For the dynamics used below this holds because the positions are periodic and $\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}$ is compactly supported or decays at least exponentially in every other coordinate, so every observable of polynomial growth is admissible. For a fixed value $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ , the Zwanzig projection maps an observable, also called a phase function, $f(\mathbf{z})$ to its average over $\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}$ conditional on $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{a}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}f \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Omega(\mathbf{a})}\int\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}(\mathbf{z})\,\delta(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})-\mathbf{a})f(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}, \displaystyle\Omega(\mathbf{a}) \displaystyle=\int\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}(\mathbf{z})\,\delta(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})-\mathbf{a})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}. $$

Here $\Omega(\mathbf{a})$ is the equilibrium probability density of the resolved observables. Where $\Omega>0$ , the free energy at fixed temperature $T>0$ is

$$ \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{a})=-k_{\mathrm{B}}T\ln\Omega(\mathbf{a}). $$

Here $T$ is the temperature of the ensemble $\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}$ , or any fixed positive constant when $\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}$ is microcanonical. It enters the exact relations below only through $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathcal{F}$ together, in a combination that does not depend on it. For any admissible function $h$ of the resolved observables, conditional expectation gives

$$ \mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}[h(\mathbf{A})f]=h(\mathbf{a})\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}f. $$

Evaluating the conditional average at $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})$ defines the projection on observables and its complement:

$$ \mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}f=\left.\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}f\right|_{\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})},\qquad\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}=1-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}, $$

so that, by eq. 4, $\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}^{2}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}=\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}=0$ . We assume that the operator evolutions $e^{t\mathcal{L}}$ and $e^{t\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}\mathcal{L}}$ exist on the observables used below.

The resolved variables then obey the standard generalized Langevin equation of the projection-operator formalism [2, 3, 1, 4, 5].

#### Theorem 1 (Generalized Langevin equation (GLE)).

Under eq. 1 and the existence and regularity assumptions stated above, the resolved trajectory satisfies

$$ \partial_{t}\mathbf{A}(t)=\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{A}(t))+\int_{0}^{t}\!\,\mathrm{d}s\,\left[k_{\mathrm{B}}T\,\nabla_{\mathbf{a}}\cdot\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{a},s)-\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{a},s)\nabla_{\mathbf{a}}\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{a})\right]_{\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{A}(t-s)}+\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(t,\mathbf{z}), $$

with the drift, the fluctuating force and the memory kernel given by

$$ \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{a})=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathcal{L}\mathbf{A},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(t,\mathbf{z})=\big(e^{t\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}\mathcal{L}}\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}\mathcal{L}\mathbf{A}\big)(\mathbf{z}), $$

$$ \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{a},s)=\frac{1}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\,\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\left[\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(s,\cdot)\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(0,\cdot)^{\mathsf{T}}\right]. $$

The fluctuating force has zero conditional mean at every admissible resolved value,

$$ \mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(t,\cdot)=\mathbf{0}. $$

For component indices $\mu,\nu=1,\ldots,m$ , the divergence acts on the second matrix index:

$$ (\nabla_{\mathbf{a}}\cdot\mathbf{K})_{\mu}=\sum_{\nu=1}^{m}\partial_{a_{\nu}}K_{\mu\nu}. $$

### S1.2 Application to density fields

We consider molecular dynamics of $N_{\alpha}$ atoms of each species $\alpha$ in a periodic cell $D$ of volume $V$ , so $\mathbf{z}$ comprises the particle positions and momenta. Periodic boundary conditions are assumed throughout this section, so all fields are periodic and integrations by parts over $D$ produce no boundary terms. For Hamiltonian dynamics in the microcanonical (NVE) ensemble this is the whole state space. For canonical (NVT) dynamics generated by a Nosé–Hoover thermostat [6], $\mathbf{z}$ also contains the thermostat variables, so the state space is the extended phase space of that scheme, on which the dynamics is deterministic.

For the density-field specialization below the cell is fixed, so particle $j$ of species $\alpha$ and mass $m_{\alpha}$ evolves by $\dot{\mathbf{r}}_{j}^{\alpha}=\mathbf{v}_{j}^{\alpha}=\mathbf{p}_{j}^{\alpha}/m_{\alpha}$ . For species $\alpha$ with $N_{\alpha}$ particles and every reciprocal-lattice wavevector $\mathbf{k}$ of the cell $D$ , define the retained Fourier coefficients

$$ \hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(\mathbf{z})=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\alpha}}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\alpha}},&|\mathbf{k}|\leq k_{\mathrm{cut}},\\[6.0pt]
0,&|\mathbf{k}|>k_{\mathrm{cut}}.\end{cases} $$

Within the cutoff these are the Fourier coefficients of the microscopic number density $\sum_{j}\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\alpha})$ . Since the positions are real,

$$ \hat{\rho}_{-\mathbf{k},\alpha}=\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}^{*},\qquad\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{0},\alpha}=N_{\alpha}. $$

Let $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(\mathbf{z})=(\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(\mathbf{z}))_{|\mathbf{k}|\leq k_{\mathrm{cut}},\,\alpha}$ be the vector of retained coefficients. Along a microscopic trajectory, write $\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(t)=\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(\mathbf{Z}(t))$ . The resolved density field is the inverse series of these coefficients, and its transform returns them,

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r},t) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(t)e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}, \displaystyle\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(t) \displaystyle=\int_{D}\rho_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r},t)e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}. $$

The sum is finite by eq. 11, so $\rho_{\alpha}$ is real and band-limited, and it shares its retained Fourier coefficients with the microscopic density while its higher ones vanish. The cutoff sets the spatial resolution. We write $\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r},t)=(\rho_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r},t))_{\alpha}$ for the vector of species density fields. For any field $f$ on $D$ , let $\Pi$ keep its retained Fourier coefficients,

$$ (\Pi f)(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{|\mathbf{k}|\leq k_{\mathrm{cut}}}\hat{f}(\mathbf{k})\,e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}},\qquad\hat{f}(\mathbf{k})=\int_{D}f(\mathbf{r})\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}, $$

so that $\boldsymbol{\rho}=\Pi\boldsymbol{\rho}$ .

We apply Theorem 1 with $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})=\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(\mathbf{z})$ and write $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t)=\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(\mathbf{Z}(t))$ . The fixed resolved value is still denoted by $\mathbf{a}$ . The entries of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ are not functionally independent, since eq. 12 ties $\hat{\rho}_{-\mathbf{k},\alpha}$ to $\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}$ and fixes the zero modes. Following Zubarev and Morozov [7], the independent variables are the real and imaginary parts of $\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}$ over a half-space of wavevectors with $\mathbf{k}\neq\mathbf{0}$ . As in Zubarev and Morozov [7], we assume these variables to be functionally independent, so that the hypotheses of Theorem 1 apply to them. Every integral over $\mathbf{a}$ and every derivative $\partial_{a_{\nu}}$ below is taken with respect to them, while the formulas are written in the complex coefficients over the full band for brevity. For $|\mathbf{k}|\leq k_{\mathrm{cut}}$ , the chain rule gives

$$ \mathcal{L}\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}=-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\alpha}}\mathbf{v}_{j}^{\alpha}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\alpha}}, $$

which is odd under reversal of all momenta, whereas $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ and $\rho^{\mathrm{eq}}$ are even. Reversing the momenta in eq. 2 therefore gives $\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathcal{L}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathcal{L}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ , so the drift vanishes,

$$ \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{a})=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathcal{L}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=\mathbf{0}. $$

Substituting into eq. 6 yields

$$ \partial_{t}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\!\,\mathrm{d}s\,\Big[k_{\mathrm{B}}T\,\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\cdot\mathbf{K}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t-s),s\big)-\mathbf{K}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t-s),s\big)\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\mathcal{F}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t-s)\big)\Big]+\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(t,\mathbf{z}). $$

Here $\mathbf{K}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t-s),s\big)$ is the memory kernel, which describes how past density configurations affect the current evolution of the field. It is a matrix on the independent real density-mode indices. Derivatives with respect to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ act on the resolved-state argument before evaluation at the displayed state, and the divergence acts on the second matrix index as in eq. 10.

The fluctuating force $\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(t,\mathbf{z})$ and the memory kernel account for the eliminated momenta and density modes above $k_{\mathrm{cut}}$ . At a fixed initial resolved density $\mathbf{a}$ , the fluctuating force has zero conditional mean by eq. 9, and satisfies the conditional fluctuation–dissipation relation [4] of eq. 8,

$$ \mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\left[\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(s,\cdot)\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(0,\cdot)^{\mathsf{T}}\right]=k_{\mathrm{B}}T\,\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{a},s). $$

The free energy is defined by eq. 3 and is a functional of the retained density fields. These relations are exact under the stated conditions and impose neither a Markov assumption nor Gaussian noise.

### S1.3 From the GLE to the mesoscopic model

Equation 16 is exact, but evaluating its memory kernel and fluctuating force requires propagating the orthogonal dynamics, which is generally impractical [4]. We make three assumptions to obtain a tractable mesoscopic model. We retain the microscopic dynamics of section S1.2 and the density field defined in eq. 13. First, in many systems, such as simple fluids, fluid mixtures, and colloidal suspensions, the memory kernel decays on a time much shorter than the evolution of the resolved density modes [8, 9]. We therefore take the dynamics as Markovian, where the memory kernel is replaced by its time integral [2, 1, 4].

Assumption 1 (Markovian dynamics). We assume that the memory kernel and its first derivatives with respect to the resolved state decay on a time $\tau_{\mathrm{mem}}$ much shorter than the evolution time $\tau_{\mathrm{field}}$ of every retained density mode. The time integral below is assumed to converge and to allow differentiation under the integral with respect to the resolved state. We define the integrated mobility and approximate the kernel by

$$ \bar{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{a})=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{a},s)\,\mathrm{d}s,\qquad\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{a},s)\approx 2\bar{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{a})\delta(s). $$

The delta approximation is understood under time integration against slowly varying functions. We use the symmetric endpoint convention $\int_{0}^{\infty}\delta(s)\,\mathrm{d}s=1/2$ , so the one-sided kernel integral is $\bar{\mathbf{M}}$ . Only time lags $s\lesssim\tau_{\mathrm{mem}}$ contribute appreciably to the memory integral. During this interval, the density changes negligibly, so $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t-s)\approx\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t)$ . For $t\gg\tau_{\mathrm{mem}}$ , the free-energy contribution therefore becomes

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\!\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathbf{K}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t-s),s\big)\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\mathcal{F}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t-s)\big) \displaystyle\approx\left[\int_{0}^{t}\!\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathbf{K}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t),s\big)\right]\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\mathcal{F}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t)\big) \displaystyle\approx\bar{\mathbf{M}}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t)\big)\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\mathcal{F}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t)\big). $$

The first approximation freezes the density, and the second neglects the small remaining tail. The same steps apply to the divergence term, using differentiation under the integral. Thus

$$ \partial_{t}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t)\approx k_{\mathrm{B}}T\,\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\cdot\bar{\mathbf{M}}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t)\big)-\bar{\mathbf{M}}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t)\big)\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\mathcal{F}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(t)\big)+\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(t,\mathbf{z}). $$

The fluctuation–dissipation relation in eq. 17, together with the delta approximation in eq. 18, gives

$$ \mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\left[\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(s,\cdot)\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(0,\cdot)^{\mathsf{T}}\right]=k_{\mathrm{B}}T\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{a},s)\approx 2k_{\mathrm{B}}T\bar{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{a})\delta(s). $$

Before imposing the local-mobility approximation, we express the memory kernel in terms of correlations of orthogonally propagated currents. By eq. 7, $\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(t)=e^{t\mathcal{Q}\mathcal{L}}\mathcal{Q}\mathcal{L}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ , and $\mathcal{Q}\mathcal{L}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=\mathcal{L}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{z})}\mathcal{L}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=\mathcal{L}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ , since the drift vanishes by eq. 15. Together with eq. 14, written as $\mathcal{L}\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}=-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{j}}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}$ where $\hat{\mathbf{j}}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}=\sum_{j}\mathbf{v}_{j}^{\alpha}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\alpha}}$ is the microscopic current, and with the linearity of $e^{t\mathcal{Q}\mathcal{L}}$ , which commutes with the constant vector $\mathbf{k}$ , this gives $\tilde{R}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(t)=-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(t)$ with $\hat{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(t)=e^{t\mathcal{Q}\mathcal{L}}\hat{\mathbf{j}}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}$ the orthogonally propagated current. Substituting into eq. 8 gives the exact form $K_{\mathbf{k}\alpha,\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\beta}(\mathbf{a},s)=-\,\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime},s)\cdot\mathbf{k}^{\prime}$ with $\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\alpha\beta}=(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)^{-1}\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\big[\hat{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(s)\,\hat{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\beta}(0)^{\mathsf{T}}\big]$ , for every $s\geq 0$ . Provided these current correlations are time integrable, the integrated mobility of eq. 18 admits the representation

$$ \displaystyle\bar{M}_{\mathbf{k}\alpha,\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\beta} \displaystyle=-\,\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime})\cdot\mathbf{k}^{\prime}, \displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime},s)\,\mathrm{d}s=\frac{1}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\big[\hat{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(s)\,\hat{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\beta}(0)^{\mathsf{T}}\big]\,\mathrm{d}s, $$

where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}_{\alpha\beta}$ is a $3\times 3$ Cartesian tensor that depends on the resolved state $\mathbf{a}$ , and $\mathbf{1}$ below denotes the identity on the Cartesian indices. It is the double Fourier transform of a two-point tensor kernel $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime};[\boldsymbol{\rho}],T)$ , a functional of the whole density field. Explicitly, with $\mathbf{J}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r},s)=e^{s\mathcal{Q}\mathcal{L}}\sum_{j}\mathbf{v}_{j}^{\alpha}\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\alpha})$ the orthogonally propagated current field and $\hat{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(s)=\int_{D}\mathbf{J}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r},s)e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}$ its Fourier transform,

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=\iint_{D}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime};[\boldsymbol{\rho}],T)\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}-i\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\cdot\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}, \displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime};[\boldsymbol{\rho}],T) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{a}}\big[\mathbf{J}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r},s)\,\mathbf{J}_{\beta}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime},0)^{\mathsf{T}}\big]\,\mathrm{d}s, $$

where $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\alpha\beta}$ is the time-integrated correlation of the current field, and the mobility operator acts as $\boldsymbol{\mu}\mapsto-\nabla\cdot\!\int_{D}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime};[\boldsymbol{\rho}],T)\cdot\nabla^{\prime}\mu_{\beta}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}$ . The factors $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{k}^{\prime}$ express mass conservation, since every term of eq. 16 is a divergence and $\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{0},\alpha}=N_{\alpha}$ is constant. The next assumption restricts only $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}$ .

Assumption 2 (Local mobility). We restrict $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}$ in eq. 19 to the local and isotropic form $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime};[\boldsymbol{\rho}],T)=M_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r}),T)\,\mathbf{1}\,\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})$ , that is, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime})=\hat{M}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{k}^{\prime})\,\mathbf{1}$ , so that in the complex coefficients of section S1.2

$$ \displaystyle\bar{M}_{\mathbf{k}\alpha,\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\beta} \displaystyle=-(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{k}^{\prime})\,\hat{M}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{k}^{\prime}), \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{q}) \displaystyle=\int_{D}\mathbf{M}(\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r}),T)e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}. $$

$\bar{\mathbf{M}}$ is defined only for $|\mathbf{k}|,|\mathbf{k}^{\prime}|\leq k_{\mathrm{cut}}$ . Here $\mathbf{M}(\boldsymbol{\rho},T)$ is the local real-space mobility, a matrix on species indices. It is symmetric positive semidefinite and continuously differentiable in the local densities, with no dependence on density gradients or the field elsewhere. This local restriction makes the integrated mobility easier to identify from trajectory data. The density field is the one defined in eq. 13, and the same retained band is used for every species. No locality assumption is imposed on $\mathcal{F}$ . All mode sums below run over the retained wavevectors, including both $\mathbf{k}$ and $-\mathbf{k}$ .

#### Lemma 1 (Vanishing thermal drift).

Under Assumption 2, the divergence of the mode-space mobility vanishes:

$$ \nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\cdot\bar{\mathbf{M}}=\mathbf{0}. $$

#### Proof.

Equation 13 gives $\partial\rho_{\gamma}/\partial\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\beta}=V^{-1}\delta_{\gamma\beta}e^{i\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\cdot\mathbf{r}}$ . Consequently,

$$ \frac{\partial\hat{M}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{k}^{\prime})}{\partial\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\beta}}=\frac{1}{V}\int_{D}\frac{\partial M_{\alpha\beta}}{\partial\rho_{\beta}}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}=\frac{1}{V}\widehat{\frac{\partial M_{\alpha\beta}}{\partial\rho_{\beta}}}(\mathbf{k}). $$

This expression is independent of $\mathbf{k}^{\prime}$ , so

$$ \sum_{\beta,\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}\frac{\partial\bar{M}_{\mathbf{k}\alpha,\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\beta}}{\partial\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\beta}}=-\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\beta}\widehat{\frac{\partial M_{\alpha\beta}}{\partial\rho_{\beta}}}(\mathbf{k})\,\mathbf{k}\cdot\sum_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}=\mathbf{0}. $$

The last sum vanishes because the retained band contains conjugate wavevector pairs. The coordinate transformation is linear, so the divergence also vanishes in the independent real coordinates. ∎

Assumption 3 (Gaussian white noise). We assume that the eliminated variables equilibrate rapidly conditional on the current density, and replace the exact force by a white noise $\hat{\mathbf{R}}(t)$ in the mode coordinates of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ that is zero-mean and Gaussian conditional on the current state $\mathbf{a}$ , with conditional covariance

$$ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat{\mathbf{R}}(t)\hat{\mathbf{R}}(t^{\prime})^{\mathsf{T}}\,\middle|\,\mathbf{a}\right]=2k_{\mathrm{B}}T\bar{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{a})\delta(t-t^{\prime}), $$

Such a process can be obtained in real space as follows. Let $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ be a zero-mean Gaussian space-time white noise with

$$ \mathbb{E}[\xi_{\alpha i}(\mathbf{r},t)\xi_{\beta j}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})]=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta_{ij}\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\delta(t-t^{\prime}), $$

where $i,j$ are Cartesian components, and set

$$ \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r},t)=\nabla\cdot\left[\sqrt{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T\mathbf{M}(\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r}),T)}\,\boldsymbol{\xi}(\mathbf{r},t)\right], $$

with $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ the field of the current resolved state and the square root the symmetric positive semidefinite one, which exists by Assumption 2. Its Fourier coefficients are retained only for $|\mathbf{k}|\leq k_{\mathrm{cut}}$ ,

$$ \hat{R}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(t)=i\mathbf{k}\cdot\sum_{\gamma}\int_{D}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\left[\sqrt{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T\mathbf{M}(\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r}),T)}\right]_{\alpha\gamma}\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\gamma}(\mathbf{r},t)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}. $$

Conditional on $\mathbf{a}$ , they are zero-mean and jointly Gaussian, being linear in $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ at fixed $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ , and eqs. 23 and 21 give

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{R}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(t)\hat{R}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\beta}(t^{\prime})\,\middle|\,\mathbf{a}\right] \displaystyle=-2k_{\mathrm{B}}T(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{k}^{\prime})\int_{D}M_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r}),T)e^{-i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{k}^{\prime})\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\,\delta(t-t^{\prime}) \displaystyle=2k_{\mathrm{B}}T\bar{M}_{\mathbf{k}\alpha,\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\beta}(\mathbf{a})\delta(t-t^{\prime}), $$

which is eq. 22.

Using Lemma 1, the three assumptions give

$$ \partial_{t}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=-\bar{\mathbf{M}}\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\mathcal{F}+\hat{\mathbf{R}}(t), $$

interpreted in the Itô sense.

#### Theorem 2 (Conservative mesoscopic model).

Under Assumptions 1–3, in real space eq. 25 reads

$$ \partial_{t}\boldsymbol{\rho}=\Pi\left\{\nabla\cdot\left[\mathbf{M}(\boldsymbol{\rho},T)\nabla\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}}{\delta\boldsymbol{\rho}}\right]+\nabla\cdot\left[\sqrt{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T\mathbf{M}(\boldsymbol{\rho},T)}\,\boldsymbol{\xi}\right]\right\}. $$

#### Proof.

We compare the retained Fourier coefficients of eq. 26 with the mode equation eq. 25.

1. Free-energy derivative. Write $\mu_{\alpha}=\delta\mathcal{F}/\delta\rho_{\alpha}$ for the zero-mean variational derivative in the retained field space. Substituting the Fourier series of an admissible density variation gives

$$ \displaystyle\delta\mathcal{F} \displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha}\int_{D}\mu_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r})\delta\rho_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\alpha,\mathbf{q}}\delta\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{q},\alpha}\int_{D}\mu_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r})e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\alpha,\mathbf{q}}\hat{\mu}_{\alpha}(-\mathbf{q})\delta\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{q},\alpha}. $$

The positive exponential gives the coefficient at $-\mathbf{q}$ . Comparing with the differential of $\mathcal{F}$ , with the complex coefficients treated as independent, yields

$$ \frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{q},\alpha}}=\frac{1}{V}\hat{\mu}_{\alpha}(-\mathbf{q}). $$

2. Deterministic term. Substituting eqs. 21 and 27 into the mode drift gives

$$ \displaystyle-\sum_{\beta,\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}\bar{M}_{\mathbf{k}\alpha,\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\beta}\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\beta}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\beta,\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{k}^{\prime})\hat{M}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{k}^{\prime})\hat{\mu}_{\beta}(-\mathbf{k}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\beta,\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{q})\hat{M}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{q})\hat{\mu}_{\beta}(\mathbf{q}), $$

where the last line uses $\mathbf{q}=-\mathbf{k}^{\prime}$ . To identify this expression, Fourier transform the real-space flux. Since $\nabla\mu_{\beta}=V^{-1}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}i\mathbf{q}\hat{\mu}_{\beta}(\mathbf{q})e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{M_{\alpha\beta}\nabla\mu_{\beta}}(\mathbf{k}) \displaystyle=\int_{D}M_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r}),T)\nabla\mu_{\beta}(\mathbf{r})e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}i\mathbf{q}\hat{\mu}_{\beta}(\mathbf{q})\int_{D}M_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r}),T)e^{-i(\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{q})\cdot\mathbf{r}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}i\mathbf{q}\hat{M}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{q})\hat{\mu}_{\beta}(\mathbf{q}). $$

Taking the divergence multiplies this coefficient by $i\mathbf{k}\cdot$ . Thus $i^{2}=-1$ and the sum over $\beta$ give exactly eq. 28. Here $\mu_{\beta}$ lies in the retained band, but the local function $M_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{\rho},T)$ is not truncated before multiplication. Its coefficient at $\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{q}$ may lie outside that band.

The noise term of eq. 26 is eq. 24 by definition. Inverse transformation reconstructs the rate as

$$ \partial_{t}\rho_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r},t)=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\left[i\mathbf{k}\cdot\sum_{\beta}\widehat{M_{\alpha\beta}\nabla\mu_{\beta}}(\mathbf{k})+\hat{R}_{\mathbf{k},\alpha}(t)\right]. $$

This is eq. 26, the projection $\Pi$ coming from the retained-band indices of $\bar{\mathbf{M}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ in Assumptions 2 and 3. ∎

In the main text eq. 26 is written without $\Pi$ , as is customary for phase-field equations. The projection is nevertheless always in force, since the state is stored as the retained Fourier coefficients and the equation is solved in Fourier space, with the nonlinear terms evaluated in real space and their retained coefficients taken, which is eq. 29.

#### Theorem 3 (Mass conservation and invariant equilibrium).

The model in eq. 26 preserves every $N_{\alpha}$ and admits the invariant probability density

$$ p_{\mathrm{eq}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})=\exp\left[-\frac{\mathcal{F}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\right]{}=\Omega(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}), $$

the equilibrium marginal of eq. 2, normalized by eq. 3.

#### Proof.

The integral of a periodic divergence is zero, so

$$ \,\mathrm{d}\int_{D}\rho_{\alpha}(\mathbf{r},t)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}=0. $$

Read in the Itô sense, eq. 25 has drift $-\bar{\mathbf{M}}\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\mathcal{F}$ and diffusion matrix $k_{\mathrm{B}}T\bar{\mathbf{M}}$ , half the covariance in eq. 22. Its Fokker–Planck equation for the density $p$ of the real mode coordinates is

$$ \partial_{t}p=\sum_{i}\partial_{i}\Big[\big(\bar{\mathbf{M}}\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\mathcal{F}\big)_{i}p\Big]+k_{\mathrm{B}}T\sum_{i,j}\partial_{i}\partial_{j}\big(\bar{M}_{ij}p\big)=\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\cdot\left[\bar{\mathbf{M}}\left(p\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\mathcal{F}+k_{\mathrm{B}}T\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}p\right)\right], $$

where $\sum_{j}\partial_{j}\bar{M}_{ij}=0$ by Lemma 1. Substituting eq. 30 gives

$$ p_{\mathrm{eq}}\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\mathcal{F}+k_{\mathrm{B}}T\nabla_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}p_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathbf{0}, $$

so the probability current vanishes and $\partial_{t}p_{\mathrm{eq}}=0$ . ∎

## S2 Numerical methods

We describe the two-species solver used for hydrogen–helium (H–He) and iron–boron (Fe–B), followed by the scalar implementation used for the Lennard-Jones mixture, and then the equilibrium density under an external potential. All mesoscopic simulations reported here include thermal noise. The same integration scheme can also be used for deterministic dynamics by omitting the stochastic contribution.

### S2.1 Dynamics

#### Discretization.

We use a pseudospectral method on a periodic grid and represent the two density fields by their nonredundant Fourier coefficients $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(\mathbf{k})$ . For simulations initialized from molecular dynamics, we coarse-grain the measured modes, normalize them by the system volume and map them onto the Fourier grid. The helium-rain simulation starts from the prescribed state described in Section S3. At each step, we differentiate the local free energy to obtain the local chemical potentials and evaluate the nonlocal contribution as $\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{k})\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(\mathbf{k})$ . This matrix–vector product replaces direct real-space convolution, and the transformed kernel can be precomputed for a fixed kernel and grid. We compute the chemical-potential gradients spectrally, multiply them by the local mobility $\mathbf{M}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\rho},T)$ in real space and evaluate the resulting flux divergence spectrally.

#### Time integration.

We use a first-order implicit–explicit (IMEX) scheme based on the reference linear operator

$$ \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{k})=|\mathbf{k}|^{2}\mathbf{M}_{\theta}(\bar{\boldsymbol{\rho}},T)\mathbf{H}_{\theta}(\mathbf{k}), $$

where $\bar{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ is the mean initial density and $\mathbf{H}_{\theta}(\mathbf{k})$ is the Fourier-space Hessian of the learned free-energy functional $\mathcal{F}_{\theta}$ , evaluated at this uniform reference state. Writing $\hat{\mathbf{N}}$ for the Fourier transform of the full deterministic term $\nabla\cdot[\mathbf{M}_{\theta}\nabla\boldsymbol{\mu}]$ , we split it as

$$ \hat{\mathbf{N}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})=-\mathbf{B}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}+\big[\hat{\mathbf{N}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})+\mathbf{B}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\big]. $$

The first term is treated implicitly and the bracketed remainder explicitly. The added and subtracted linear terms cancel, so the reference linearization does not replace the full nonlinear dynamics. Including the stochastic contribution gives

$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{\,n+1}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{\,n}+\Delta t\,\big[\mathbf{I}+\Delta t\,\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{k})\big]^{-1}\big(\hat{\mathbf{N}}^{\,n}+\hat{\mathbf{g}}^{\,n}\big), $$

where $\hat{\mathbf{N}}^{\,n}$ is evaluated at the current density fields and $\hat{\mathbf{g}}^{\,n}$ is the stochastic contribution defined below. Each Fourier mode requires only an independent $2\times 2$ linear solve, performed analytically, rather than a nonlinear solve over the full spatial grid. In the absence of noise and additional state projections, the update preserves the stationary solutions of the deterministic dynamics.

#### Stochastic contribution.

At each step, we draw independent standard normal variables $w_{jd}(\mathbf{r})$ for each grid cell, species $j$ and Cartesian direction $d$ . We construct the stochastic flux from a Cholesky factor of the local mobility,

$$ \zeta_{id}(\mathbf{r})=\sqrt{\frac{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{\Delta V\,\Delta t}}\;\mathsf{L}_{ij}\big(\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r})\big)\,w_{jd}(\mathbf{r}),\qquad\mathsf{L}\mathsf{L}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{M}_{\theta}\big(\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r}),T\big), $$

where $\Delta V$ is the grid-cell volume and repeated species indices are summed. This construction preserves the cross-species noise correlations specified by the off-diagonal mobility. We evaluate the flux divergence spectrally and apply the Gaussian filter $\exp(-|\mathbf{k}|^{2}\sigma^{2}/2)$ used to define the coarse-grained fields. The resulting Fourier contribution is $\hat{\mathbf{g}}^{\,n}$ , whose zero mode is set to zero to conserve the number of each species. Evaluating the noise amplitude at the beginning of each step gives a semi-implicit Euler–Maruyama discretization in the Itô convention.

#### Lennard-Jones implementation.

For the Lennard-Jones mixture, we use a scalar version of the same scheme to evolve the composition field, which is stored in real space. The reference linear operator is the Cahn–Hilliard gradient-energy stabilizer of the semi-implicit Fourier-spectral method [10, 11],

$$ B(\mathbf{k})=\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}\,M_{\max}\,|\mathbf{k}|^{4}, $$

where $\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\widehat{W}_{\theta}^{\prime\prime}(0)$ is the gradient-energy coefficient given by the small- $k$ expansion of the learned kernel, or the gradient coefficient $\kappa$ of the baselines, and $M_{\max}$ is the maximum of the local mobility over the domain at the current step. It replaces the learned Hessian $\mathbf{H}_{\theta}(\mathbf{k})$ of the two-species scheme. The noise construction, Gaussian filtering and zero-mode constraint follow the procedure above, with $\sigma=1.5\,\sigma_{AA}$ .

### S2.2 Thermodynamics

The external potential enters $\mathcal{F}_{\theta}$ through the coupling term $\int\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\rho}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}$ of Methods. At fixed chemical potentials $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ , the equilibrium density minimizes the grand potential,

$$ \min_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ \Big\{\mathcal{F}_{\theta}([\boldsymbol{\rho}],T)-\boldsymbol{\mu}\!\cdot\!\!\int\!\boldsymbol{\rho}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\Big\}. $$

In the canonical ensemble, the particle numbers $\mathbf{N}$ are fixed and the equilibrium density minimizes $\mathcal{F}_{\theta}$ subject to particle conservation,

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ \mathcal{F}_{\theta}([\boldsymbol{\rho}],T), \displaystyle\text{subject to}\quad\int\!\boldsymbol{\rho}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{N}. $$

Both variational problems give the stationarity condition

$$ \frac{\delta\mathcal{F}_{\theta}([\boldsymbol{\rho}],T)}{\delta\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r})}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\qquad\text{for all }\mathbf{r}, $$

which is the stationarity condition of the main text with the external potential retained. The chemical potentials are prescribed in the grand canonical ensemble and arise as Lagrange multipliers enforcing particle conservation in the canonical ensemble.

## S3 Experimental details and further results

### S3.1 Symmetric binary Lennard-Jones mixture

#### Model form.

The Lennard-Jones mixture is nearly incompressible, so the local total density $\rho_{A}+\rho_{B}$ remains $1.0\,\sigma_{AA}^{-3}$ at every point, and the free energy and mobility depend only on the composition field $x_{A}=\rho_{A}/(\rho_{A}+\rho_{B})$ . We impose symmetry under exchange of species $A$ and $B$ . The free energy comprises the parameter-free ideal part and the learned excess part,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{id}} \displaystyle=\int f_{\mathrm{id}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r},\qquad f_{\mathrm{id}}=T\big[x_{A}\ln x_{A}+(1-x_{A})\ln(1-x_{A})\big], \displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{exc},\theta} \displaystyle=\int f_{\mathrm{loc},\theta}(x_{A},T)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}+\tfrac{1}{2}\iint\big[x_{A}(\mathbf{r})-\tfrac{1}{2}\big]\,W_{\theta}(\lvert\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rvert)\,\big[x_{A}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})-\tfrac{1}{2}\big]\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}, \displaystyle f_{\mathrm{loc},\theta} \displaystyle=u_{0,\theta}(x_{A})+T\,u_{1,\theta}(x_{A}). $$

The local energy $u_{0,\theta}$ is an even Taylor polynomial in $x_{A}-\tfrac{1}{2}$ , with terms of orders $2$ , $4$ , $6$ and $8$ . The function $u_{1,\theta}$ is an input-convex neural network with one input and width $32$ , symmetrized under $x_{A}\to 1-x_{A}$ . The temperature-independent radial kernel $W_{\theta}(r)$ is represented by a multilayer perceptron with two layers of width $16$ , multiplied by a quintic envelope that vanishes at $R_{\mathrm{cut}}=3.0\,\sigma_{AA}$ .

The mobility is $M_{\theta}(x_{A},T)=\gamma\,x_{A}(1-x_{A})\,c_{\theta}(T)$ , where $c_{\theta}(T)=\exp[-E_{a}(1/T-1/T_{\mathrm{ref}})]$ and $T_{\mathrm{ref}}=1.65$ . Both $\gamma$ and $E_{a}$ are learned.

#### Training and validation data.

The datasets and simulation conditions are summarized in table S1. Slab trajectories provide the dynamical training data. The trajectories at $T=1.20$ are held out from training and model selection and used only for validation. Homogeneous cubes provide the mobility and bulk anchors at four temperatures, $T=1.50$ , $1.60$ , $1.70$ and $1.80$ , with measurements averaged over three independent seeds at each temperature. Quench trajectories are excluded from training and used only to assess the predicted coarsening dynamics.

The dynamical residual compares an estimate of the time derivative over a window of frames with the model drift averaged over the same window. For fields $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{j}$ saved at interval $\Delta$ and a window centered at frame $j_{c}$ , the time derivative is estimated as

$$ \widehat{\partial_{t}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}(t_{j_{c}})=\frac{1}{w\Delta}\Big[\frac{1}{w}\sum_{m=1}^{w}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{j_{c}+m}-\frac{1}{w}\sum_{m=0}^{w-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{j_{c}-m}\Big]. $$

This estimator divides the difference between the mean fields over the following and preceding $w$ frames by $\delta t=w\Delta$ , the interval defined in the main text. We evaluate the model drift at $n_{s}$ evenly spaced frames within the same window and take a weighted average. The dynamical residual is the difference between this averaged drift and the estimated time derivative.

For the Lennard-Jones mixture, frames are saved every $\tau$ , and $w=25$ gives $\delta t=25\,\tau$ . Window centers are separated by $20$ frames, and the drift is evaluated at $n_{s}=5$ frames per window. The loss averages over all windows and training trajectories. To prevent strongly driven trajectories from dominating, trajectory $r$ is weighted by $w_{r}\propto 1/(m_{r}+\bar{m})$ , where $m_{r}$ is the mean squared band-limited $H^{-1}$ norm of its estimated time derivative and $\bar{m}$ is the median across trajectories.

The training loss is $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}+\lambda_{M}\mathcal{L}_{M}+\lambda_{\mathrm{bulk}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bulk}}$ , with unit weight for the dynamical term and $\lambda_{M}=\lambda_{\mathrm{bulk}}=0.01$ . We use neither a finite-wavevector static anchor nor an isobar anchor, and impose no additional constraint term for this symmetric mixture at fixed total density.

#### Domain growth.

We characterize spinodal decomposition by a length scale obtained from the inverse first moment of the composition spectrum,

$$ L(t)=2\pi\,\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{k}}S(\mathbf{k},t)}{\sum_{\mathbf{k}}|\mathbf{k}|\,S(\mathbf{k},t)}, $$

where $S(\mathbf{k},t)=|\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{k},t)|^{2}$ . For molecular dynamics, $\hat{\psi}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},A}-\hat{\rho}_{\mathbf{k},B})$ , with the Gaussian coarse-graining filter applied analytically to the bare particle modes. For the ab initio phase-field (AIPF) model, $\hat{\psi}$ is the Fourier amplitude of the already coarse-grained composition field. This construction gives the same estimator for both descriptions. The sums include individual modes on the box’s wavevector lattice over $0<|\mathbf{k}|\leq 1.5\,\sigma_{AA}^{-1}$ . We avoid shell averaging because replacing wavevectors by shell centers imposes an artificial upper limit on $L(t)$ that is reached during these runs.

We extract the growth exponent $\beta$ from the slope of $\log L$ against $\log t$ , using a window after the initial transient and before finite-size saturation. For each method, we select the half-decade with the steepest slope within this interval. The quoted uncertainty represents the scatter across independent seeds. At the present box size, the local slope does not reach a plateau. The fitted $\beta$ is therefore an effective, window-dependent exponent rather than an asymptotic growth law. Distinguishing candidate asymptotic laws would require a box several times larger.

We evaluate the growth exponent at five quench temperatures between $1.10$ and $1.30$ (fig. S1). Agreement is closest at $T=1.20$ , the case shown in the main text. The largest discrepancy occurs at $T=1.10$ , where the AIPF model gives $\beta=0.161\pm 0.020$ , compared with $0.293\pm 0.024$ from molecular dynamics.

### S3.2 Iron–boron melt

#### Model form.

We describe the melt by the species-density fields $\boldsymbol{\rho}=(\rho_{\mathrm{B}},\rho_{\mathrm{Fe}})$ . The free-energy functional comprises the parameter-free ideal contribution $k_{\mathrm{B}}T\sum_{\alpha}\int\rho_{\alpha}(\ln\rho_{\alpha}-1)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}$ , with $\rho_{\alpha}$ in Å-3, and the learned excess contribution

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{exc},\theta} \displaystyle=\int f_{\mathrm{loc},\theta}(\boldsymbol{\rho},T)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}+\tfrac{1}{2}\iint\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathbf{W}_{\theta}(\lvert\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rvert)\,\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}. $$

The ideal contribution differs from the form given in Methods by $k_{\mathrm{B}}T\sum_{\alpha}\int\rho_{\alpha}\ln\Lambda_{\alpha}^{3}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}$ , where $\Lambda_{\alpha}$ is the thermal wavelength of species $\alpha$ . This term is linear in the densities at fixed temperature and changes neither the pressure nor the free energy of mixing. The local function $f_{\mathrm{loc},\theta}$ is a multilayer perceptron of the two densities and the temperature, with architecture $3\to 64\to 64\to 64\to 64\to 1$ and GELU activations. The temperature-independent, symmetric $2\times 2$ kernel contains three radial components corresponding to B–B, B–Fe and Fe–Fe interactions. Each component is represented by a $1\to 16\to 16\to 1$ perceptron of the separation, multiplied by a quintic envelope that vanishes at $R_{\mathrm{cut}}=4.5\,$ Å.

The mobility is parametrized as $\mathbf{M}_{\theta}=\mathbf{C}_{\theta}^{1/2}\mathbf{D}^{1/2}\mathbf{L}_{\theta}\mathbf{L}_{\theta}^{\!\top}\mathbf{D}^{1/2}\mathbf{C}_{\theta}^{1/2}$ , with $\mathbf{D}=\mathrm{diag}(\rho_{\mathrm{B}},\rho_{\mathrm{Fe}})$ and $\mathbf{C}_{\theta}=\mathrm{diag}\big(c_{\mathrm{B},\theta}(T),c_{\mathrm{Fe},\theta}(T)\big)$ . A $2\to 16\to 16\to 3$ perceptron of the densities supplies the lower-triangular factor $\mathbf{L}_{\theta}$ , which makes $\mathbf{M}_{\theta}$ positive semidefinite by construction. The temperature dependence is $c_{\alpha,\theta}(T)=\exp[-E_{\alpha}(1/k_{\mathrm{B}}T-1/k_{\mathrm{B}}T_{\mathrm{ref}})]$ , with $T_{\mathrm{ref}}=1800\,$ K and one learned activation energy $E_{\alpha}$ for each species.

#### Training data and state selection.

The molecular-dynamics datasets cover $0$ , $5$ and $10\,$ GPa, with the same grid of $145$ state points at each pressure (table S2). The temperatures are $T\in\{1200,\allowbreak 1300,\allowbreak 1400,\allowbreak 1500,\allowbreak 1600,\allowbreak 1700,\allowbreak 1800,\allowbreak 1900,\allowbreak 2000,\allowbreak 2300,\allowbreak 2600\}\,$ K. We classify each state from the concentration structure factor $S_{cc}(k,t)$ . A state is spinodal when $\Gamma_{\mathrm{MD}}\leq 0.35$ and coarsening is confirmed on a trajectory of at least $200\,$ ps. Coarsening requires that the peak of $S_{cc}(k)$ either moves toward the smallest wavevector of the box or stays at a finite wavevector while its amplitude grows, and that the peak exceeds five times the background without declining at the end of the trajectory. A state is stable when three conditions hold. First, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{MD}}\geq 1$ . Second, the Ornstein–Zernike estimate of $S_{cc}(0)$ rests on at least $100$ independent samples of the long-wavelength composition modes, which corresponds to a relative error of $10\,\%$ . Third, the long-wavelength band $k\leq 0.52\,$ Å-1 shows no growth over the second half of the trajectory, meaning that the late-to-early change in its amplitude is within $1.5$ standard deviations and the series is stationary. All other states are classified as unresolved.

States are excluded from all trajectory-based loss terms if $T\leq 1300\,$ K or if the slower species diffuses less than one bond length over the trajectory, as determined by $6\min(D_{\mathrm{B}},D_{\mathrm{Fe}})\,t<9\,$ Å2. The remaining trajectories contribute to the dynamical loss. Stable states that also satisfy the anchor-selection threshold provide the static and mobility anchors. #### Training objective and constraints.

The dynamical residual uses the estimator of eq. 31, with $w=100$ frames saved every $0.1\,$ ps, giving $\delta t=10\,$ ps. Window centers are spaced every $40$ frames, and $n_{s}=5$ . All trajectories carry equal weight. The model is evaluated at states midway between consecutive frames.

The loss is $\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{\mathrm{dyn}}\sum_{s}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}^{(s)}+\lambda_{M}\mathcal{L}_{M}+\lambda_{S}\mathcal{L}_{S}+\lambda_{\mathrm{bulk}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bulk}}+\lambda_{P}\mathcal{L}_{P}+\lambda_{W}\mathcal{L}_{W}$ . The dynamical term sums the contributions from nonequilibrium and stable runs at all three pressures, with $\lambda_{\mathrm{dyn}}=1.5\times 10^{4}$ . The remaining weights are $\lambda_{M}=0.5$ , $\lambda_{S}=0.03$ , $\lambda_{\mathrm{bulk}}=0.01$ , $\lambda_{P}=5.0$ and $\lambda_{W}=0.3$ . The hinge penalty $\mathcal{L}_{W}$ penalizes violations of the lower bound $\kappa k^{2}$ on $\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{\theta}(k)-\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{\theta}(0)$ , with $\kappa=2.0$ .

We impose no convexity penalty on the local free energy and no prior on the thermodynamic factor. This allows the local free energy to become nonconvex in the boron-rich region where the instability is observed.

The isobar anchor compares the model’s Euler pressure with the target pressure of each equation-of-state state point,

$$ \mathcal{L}_{P}=\Big\langle\Big(\frac{P_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\rho},T)-P_{\mathrm{meas}}}{\max(|P_{\mathrm{meas}}|,P_{\mathrm{ref}})}\Big)^{\!2}\Big\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\rho},T}, $$

where $P_{\mathrm{ref}}=10\,$ GPa and the denominator avoids division by zero at ambient pressure. All three target pressures lie at or below $P_{\mathrm{ref}}$ , so the same denominator applies to every state and the penalty measures the squared absolute pressure residual in units of $P_{\mathrm{ref}}$ .

#### Anchor measurements.

Configurations are saved every $0.1\,$ ps. We evaluate the apparent mobility at lags of one to ten frames, fit its diffusive branch linearly in $\Delta t$ for each wavevector shell and extrapolate to $\Delta t=0$ . The resulting shell intercepts are then extrapolated linearly in $k^{2}$ to obtain the zero-wavevector mobility. The static anchor uses measured shells up to $k=1.5\,$ Å-1, whereas the Ornstein–Zernike fit uses $k<0.8\,$ Å-1.

#### Model form.

We describe the mixture by the species-density fields $\boldsymbol{\rho}=(\rho_{\mathrm{H}},\rho_{\mathrm{He}})$ . The free-energy functional comprises the parameter-free ideal contribution $k_{\mathrm{B}}T\sum_{\alpha}\int\rho_{\alpha}(\ln\rho_{\alpha}-1)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}$ , with $\rho_{\alpha}$ in Å-3, and the learned excess contribution

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{exc},\theta} \displaystyle=\int f_{\mathrm{loc},\theta}(\boldsymbol{\rho},T)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}+\tfrac{1}{2}\iint\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathbf{W}_{\theta}(\lvert\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rvert)\,\boldsymbol{\rho}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}, \displaystyle f_{\mathrm{loc},\theta} \displaystyle=u_{0,\theta}(\boldsymbol{\rho})+k_{\mathrm{B}}T\,u_{1,\theta}(\boldsymbol{\rho})+k_{\mathrm{B}}T\ln\frac{T}{T_{\mathrm{ref}}}\,u_{2,\theta}(\boldsymbol{\rho}). $$

The ideal contribution uses the same convention as for the iron–boron melt. The local functions $u_{0,\theta}$ , $u_{1,\theta}$ and $u_{2,\theta}$ are multilayer perceptrons with architecture $2\to h\to h\to 1$ , GELU activations and widths $h=16$ , $32$ and $16$ , respectively. The reference temperature is $T_{\mathrm{ref}}=8000\,$ K. Before training, the basis function $k_{\mathrm{B}}T\ln(T/T_{\mathrm{ref}})$ is orthogonalized against $1$ and $k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ over $9000$ – $12\,000\,$ K. This redistributes its constant and linear parts among $u_{0,\theta}$ , $u_{1,\theta}$ and $u_{2,\theta}$ without changing the space spanned by the basis functions. The temperature-independent, symmetric $2\times 2$ kernel $\mathbf{W}_{\theta}$ contains three radial components corresponding to H–H, H–He and He–He interactions. Each component is represented by a $1\to 16\to 16\to 1$ perceptron of the separation, multiplied by a quintic envelope that vanishes at $R_{\mathrm{cut}}=4.5\,$ Å.

The mobility is parametrized as $\mathbf{M}_{\theta}=\mathbf{D}^{1/2}\mathbf{L}_{\theta}\mathbf{L}_{\theta}^{\!\top}\mathbf{D}^{1/2}$ , where $\mathbf{D}=\mathrm{diag}(\rho_{\mathrm{H}},\rho_{\mathrm{He}})$ and a perceptron of the densities supplies the lower-triangular factor $\mathbf{L}_{\theta}$ . This parametrization makes $\mathbf{M}_{\theta}$ positive semidefinite by construction. No explicit temperature factor is included.

#### Training objective and anchor measurements.

The loss is $\mathcal{L}=\sum_{s=1}^{8}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}^{(s)}+\lambda_{M}\mathcal{L}_{M}+\lambda_{S}\mathcal{L}_{S}+\lambda_{\mathrm{bulk}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bulk}}+\lambda_{P}\mathcal{L}_{P}+\lambda_{\mathrm{conv}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{conv}}+\lambda_{\Gamma}\mathcal{L}_{\Gamma}$ . The eight dynamical terms correspond to the slab and cube datasets at each of the four pressures and enter with unit weight. The remaining weights are $\lambda_{M}=0.5$ , $\lambda_{S}=0.01$ , $\lambda_{\mathrm{bulk}}=0.01$ , $\lambda_{P}=5.0$ , $\lambda_{\mathrm{conv}}=1.0$ and $\lambda_{\Gamma}=1.0$ . The weights were set by a coarse sweep over a few values of each, judged by the fit to the anchors, the equation of state and the dynamical residual on the training data.

Configurations are saved every $0.02\,$ ps. We evaluate the apparent mobility at lags of one to ten frames and exclude lags shorter than $0.06\,$ ps, where fast nonhydrodynamic fluctuations introduce a lag-independent contribution to the increment variance. For each wavevector shell, we fit the diffusive branch of the apparent mobility linearly in $\Delta t$ and extrapolate to $\Delta t=0$ . We then obtain $\mathbf{M}(0)$ by fitting the shell intercepts to a universal kernel shape over $k\leq 1.6\,$ Å-1, with one fitted parameter. The static anchor uses measured shells up to $k=1.5\,$ Å-1, whereas $S_{cc}(0)$ is obtained from an Ornstein–Zernike fit over $k\leq 0.9\,$ Å-1.

The isobar anchor compares the model’s Euler pressure with the target pressure of each equation-of-state state point,

$$ \mathcal{L}_{P}=\Big\langle\Big(\frac{P_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\rho},T)-P_{\mathrm{meas}}}{P_{\mathrm{meas}}}\Big)^{\!2}\Big\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\rho},T}. $$

Normalizing each residual by its target pressure gives a relative-error penalty, so that the weight $\lambda_{P}$ has the same interpretation at all four pressures.

#### Functional constraints.

Two additional one-sided penalties constrain the shape of the learned functional. They encode modeling priors and vanish wherever their respective conditions are satisfied.

The first penalizes deviations from convexity of the local free energy. Let $\lambda_{\min}$ be the smallest eigenvalue of $\partial^{2}f_{\mathrm{loc},\theta}/\partial\boldsymbol{\rho}\,\partial\boldsymbol{\rho}$ and $m$ a fixed margin. We define

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{conv}}=\big\langle\,\big[\max(0,\,m-\lambda_{\min})\big]^{2}\,\big\rangle. $$

The penalty is zero for $\lambda_{\min}\geq m$ and grows quadratically below this threshold. We estimate the average by Monte Carlo sampling. At each optimization step, we draw new points uniformly within the density trust region and uniformly in logarithmic temperature over the training range. The nonlocal kernel is excluded from this penalty. Enforcing local convexity assigns the bulk demixing instability to $\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{\theta}(0)$ rather than to the local free energy. This separation is a modeling choice.

The second penalty constrains the composition dependence of the thermodynamic factor,

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\Gamma}=\big\langle\,\big[\min(0,\,\partial^{2}\Gamma/\partial x^{2})\big]^{2}\,\big\rangle. $$

It penalizes negative curvature of $\Gamma(x)$ , with no additional margin. We evaluate $\Gamma$ from the local Hessian and $\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{\theta}(0)$ along measured equation-of-state density paths. We compute its second derivative using a five-point stencil. The average is restricted to the interior of the sampled composition range. Dilute compositions are excluded to avoid penalizing their physical curvature. Pressure and temperature paths are resampled at each optimization step.

#### Helium-rain simulation.

The helium-rain panels in the main text are obtained from a single stochastic simulation of the learned model using the Fourier pseudospectral scheme described in Section S2. We use a $192\times 192\times 512$ grid with spacing $0.70\,$ Å and periodic boundaries in all three directions. The full computational domain measures $13.4\times 13.4\times 35.8\,$ nm and corresponds to approximately $4.4$ million atoms. The gravitational potential and prescribed temperature profile are extended by reflection along the vertical direction and smoothed near the reflection planes to maintain periodicity. No reflection symmetry is imposed on the density fields or stochastic noise, so these planes do not impose reflecting boundary conditions. The main-text panels show one half of the periodic domain, measuring $13.4\times 13.4\times 17.9\,$ nm and corresponding to approximately $2.2$ million atoms.

The initial density fields are uniform, with protosolar composition $x_{\mathrm{He}}=0.089$ and total number density $0.6753\,$ Å-3, corresponding to the equilibrium density at $400\,$ GPa. Within the displayed half-domain, the fixed temperature profile increases from $3700\,$ K at the top to $3900\,$ K at the bottom and is linear away from the $8\,$ Å smoothing layers at each end. The entire domain is initially metastable, with both ends inside the binodal and outside the spinodal. The temperature profile thus produces a gradient in supersaturation without crossing a phase boundary. Gravity is imposed through an external potential linear in height, with $g=2.68\times 10^{-3}\,$ eV amu-1 Å-1, approximately $10^{14}$ times Saturn’s gravity. This value gives a Bond number of $4.00$ over the free height of $163.2\,$ Å, which is the physical height of $179.2\,$ Å minus an $8\,$ Å layer at each end over which gravity is smoothly switched off, matching the ratio of gravitational to interfacial forces in a planetary rain zone thousands of kilometers deep.

We integrate the model using the stochastic scheme described in Section S2, with a time step of $5\times 10^{-3}\,$ ps and the noise amplitude set by the fluctuation–dissipation relation. Density fields are saved every $2\,$ ps. We use a single noise seed and show the first nanosecond in the main-text panels.
